claims.overstatement: None for the part that cites this source. Three small points of wording, none an overstatement: (1) 'not the share of any one person's risk' is a fair inference from the review's population-level definition (p. 255) and its rejection of heritability as the proportion of a phenotype passed on (Box 2, p. 257); the review does not discuss individual risk in those words. (2) The review says the observed-scale heritability of an all-or-none trait is always smaller than the liability-scale value (Box 5, p. 262); the claim's 'much smaller ... when the condition is rare' is the case its example shows (schizophrenia, incidence 1%: 0.16 against 0.81) and follows from the Box 5 formula. (3) For gene-environment correlation the review says ignoring it will inflate the genetic variance (Box 1, p. 256) but for IQ twin estimates only that they might be overestimated (Box 4, p. 260); the claim's 'overstates' is acceptable as a statement about the direction of bias.
claims.note: Checked only the sentences attributed to Visscher et al. (2008); the Kendler et al. (2012) and Prom-Wormley et al. (2017) parts are not from this source. Every element of the Visscher sentences was found: ratio of variances in one population for a measurement at a particular time or age (p. 255); not genetic determination, height about 0.8 with a secular rise (p. 257); nothing about group differences or changes in the mean over time (p. 257); population-specific, in theory not transferable, in practice often similar (p. 256); changes with environment, age and measurement method (p. 261); observed against liability scale (pp. 259, 262); only three variance components from the classical twin design (p. 258); upward bias from greater shared environment of identical twins and from gene-environment correlation (pp. 256, 258, 260). Numbers from this source in the claim: 'about 0.8' for height (Box 2, p. 257, and p. 264) and 'three variance components' (p. 258), both confirmed on the rendered pages. The review discusses no drug-use, alcohol, tobacco or addiction phenotype (text searched; the only 'drug' is drug development, Box 6, p. 263), as the claim says. The review's illustrative figures are second-hand and quoted without intervals; the claim uses only the height figure, as an illustration.

anchors.extracted: Heritability is formally a ratio of variances: the proportion of the total variance in a population, for a given measurement taken at a particular time or age, attributable to variation in additive genetic values (narrow sense, h2) or in total genetic values (broad sense, H2); one number for the fraction of the variation between individuals in a population that is due to their genotypes. The introduction calls it a population parameter.

Because genetic variance (segregating alleles, their frequencies, effect sizes and mode of action) and environmental variance are specific to a population, the heritability in one population does not in theory predict that of the same trait in another; in practice heritabilities of similar traits are often remarkably similar in other populations of the same species or across species. It can differ between sexes and between early and late life (beef cattle: about 0.3 for weaning weight, 0.4 for market weight).

The standard partition assumes no genotype-environment covariance and no genotype-by-environment interaction; both are often ignored because they cannot be estimated; if present, ignoring the covariance inflates the estimated genetic variance and ignoring the interaction inflates the environmental variance.

Misconceptions: heritability is not the proportion of a phenotype handed to the next generation (genes, not phenotypes, are transmitted); a high heritability means most present variation in the population is due to genotype but not that the phenotype is fixed by the genotype, because the environment can change or be manipulated; the secular rise in human height in many populations is compatible with reported heritabilities of about 0.8 and likely reflects better nutrition and medical care.

Heritability should not be used to predict changes in a population's mean over time or differences between groups, because it is defined for one population and says nothing about environments in others (examples: the Flynn effect in IQ; US-born white men about 9 cm taller than Dutch men in the mid-19th century, Dutch men now about 5 cm taller, likely environmental).

anchors.locator: Estimation of heritability, 4th and 5th paragraphs (left column)
anchors.extracted: Bias can come from confounding (for example assortative mating and selection). The classical MZ/DZ twin design gives only three essential statistics (MZ resemblance, DZ resemblance, total phenotypic variance), so only three variance components can be estimated although many more causes can be postulated; confounding can severely bias the estimate; resemblance between parents and offspring partly due to common environment biases heritability upward.

For all-or-none (disease) traits heritability can be defined on the observed scale or on an underlying liability scale. Schizophrenia (first-degree relative risk 9, incidence 1%) and major depression (relative risk 3, incidence 3%) have similar observed-scale heritabilities (0.16 and 0.12) but very different liability-scale values (0.81 and 0.37); for risk prediction from family history or genotypes the observed 0-1 scale matters most.

Observed-scale heritability of a 0/1 trait depends on its incidence K (observed variance K(1-K)); under the liability-threshold model h2(observed) = h2 z^2/[K(1-K)]; heritability on the observed scale is always smaller than on the liability scale, at most 0.64 when K = 0.5 and h2 = 1.

For IQ, gene-environment correlation is likely, so twin heritability estimates might be overestimated; maternal (for example in utero) effects larger for MZ than for DZ twins would bias the estimate upward because equal common-environment resemblance is assumed; a meta-analysis modelling maternal effects gave narrow-sense 0.3 and broad-sense 0.5 (against twin estimates of 0.5-0.8). The box calls the view that a high heritability means a trait cannot be changed by intervention an incorrect perception.

anchors.locator: Heritability is not necessarily constant, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Heritability can change over time when genetic variance, environmental variance or the gene-environment correlation changes; the same trait can have different genetic and environmental influences over the lifetime, so the variances depend on age; heritability can be changed by changing environmental variance, even by changing the method of measurement (self-reported against clinically measured height). Examples: first-lactation milk yield from about 25% in the 1970s to about 40%; cricket wing dimorphism 0.71 in the laboratory against 0.21 in the field.

As a ratio of variances heritability does not give the size of either component; it refers to a particular population and environment and not to differences between them; as a composite measure it says nothing about individual genes. Human height heritability given as approximately 0.8 (Why are heritabilities so large?, same page).
